steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A semiconductor diode allows current to flow in one direction only; it has a forward voltage drop of about 0.7 V for silicon.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An LED (light-emitting diode) emits light when forward biased; it requires a series resistor to limit current.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has three terminals: base, collector and emitter.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An NPN transistor switches on when the base-emitter voltage exceeds ~0.7 V, allowing collector current to flow.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the typical forward voltage drop of a silicon diode? | Q: A transistor has h_FE = 100 and I_B = 50 μA. What is I_C? | Q: Why does an LED need a series resistor?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Approximately 0.7 V. | I_C = h_FE × I_B = 100 × 50 × 10⁻⁶ = 5 mA. | To limit the forward current to a safe value; without it, excessive current would destroy the LED.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always include a series resistor when calculating LED circuits. State the value of V_BE (0.7 V for silicon) before using it in calculations. For switching circuits, verify the transistor is in saturation by checking I_C < h_FE × I_B. Label base, collector and emitter clearly on any circuit diagram. Remember that a common-emitter amplifier inverts the output signal.
